quoted_clause: under case (ii) (full-square, ×1.1723) the ceiling falls to ≈16,870 linear-equivalent tok/s and the ratio becomes 2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692 ≈ 109%, and under case (iii) (causal-triangle, ×1.0861) ≈101%
observed: The case (ii) and case (iii) ratios are arithmetically wrong. Case (ii): 2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692 = 3.0198 ÷ 2.7692 = 1.0905 ≈ 109% — this one is correct. Case (iii): the text claims ≈101%, but 2 × 1.3989 ÷ 2.7692 = 2.7978 ÷ 2.7692 = 1.0103 ≈ 101% — this is also correct. HOWEVER, the case (i) ratio stated earlier is 18,400 ÷ 19,780 ≈ 93%, and the case (ii) ceiling 16,870 is inconsistent with the ×1.1723 factor: 19,780 ÷ 1.1723 = 16,872 (correct), but the ratio expression '2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692' uses 2.7692 as denominator which equals 19,780 × 1.1723 / 8333... the internal consistency of the 2.7692 denominator vs the 16,870 ceiling is unverifiable from stated inputs — the ratio numerator (2 × 1.5099 = 3.0198 PFLOP is the case (ii) prefill FLOP, but dividing a PFLOP by a tokens/s quantity is dimensionally incoherent).
evidence: The ratio '2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692' mixes units: 1.5099 is PFLOP/request (case ii prefill FLOP from Ch 22 Table 22-1), while 2.7692 appears to be a tokens/s-derived constant. The demand is 18,400 input tok/s. To get a ratio you need ceiling-in-tok/s ÷ demand-in-tok/s. Case (i): 19,780 ÷ 18,400 = 1.075 → but text says 93% (18,400÷19,780). Case (ii): ceiling 16,870 tok/s ÷ 18,400 = 0.917 = 91.7%, NOT 109%. The text's '109%' comes from 2×1.5099÷2.7692 which is a different construction entirely. The two methods (tok/s ratio vs PFLOP-based ratio) give opposite conclusions (92% vs 109%), and the text does not reconcile them. Recomputation: if ceiling falls to 16,870 tok/s under case (ii), the load ratio 18,400/16,870 = 109% — so the 109% IS the tok/s ratio (demand/ceiling), but case (i) was reported as ceiling/demand (18,400/19,780=93%). The direction of the ratio flips between case (i) [demand÷ceiling] and case (ii)/(iii) [also demand÷ceiling: 18,400÷16,870=109%, 18,400÷(19,780/1.0861)=18,400÷18,212=101%]. So actually all three are demand÷ceiling and consistent IF case (iii) ceiling = 19,780/1.0861 = 18,212. But the text says case (iii) ceiling uses ×1.0861 giving ≈101%, and 18,400/18,212 = 1.0103 ✓. The real problem: the expression '2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692' is a red herring / obfuscation that happens to equal 1.09 but is dimensionally meaningless, and 2.7692 is unexplained. This is a presentation/root-cause defect that masks whether the numbers are derived correctly.
root_cause: The ratio is expressed via an unexplained PFLOP-based formula (2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692) instead of the transparent tok/s ratio (demand ÷ ceiling). The constant 2.7692 is never defined, and the formula mixes PFLOP and tokens/s. While the final percentages (93/109/101) are internally consistent as demand÷ceiling ratios, the stated formula is dimensionally incoherent and non-reproducible, violating the book's own 'show inputs, equation, result' standard and the §3 gate-scope expectation.
correction: Replace the opaque formula with the transparent tok/s construction: case (i) 18,400÷19,780 = 93%; case (ii) 18,400÷(19,780/1.1723)=18,400÷16,872 = 109%; case (iii) 18,400÷(19,780/1.0861)=18,400÷18,212 = 101%. Define 2.7692 or delete the PFLOP expression. State explicitly that the ratio is demand÷ceiling (a load fraction >100% = infeasible).
acceptance_test: Recompute all three case ratios as demand(18,400 tok/s) ÷ ceiling(tok/s) with the ceiling explicitly derived from 19,780 ÷ factor; confirm 93%/109%/101% and that >100% is flagged as infeasible. Confirm no PFLOP/tok-s mixing remains.

observed: The event-level ledger's 'Input before call' column double-counts tool outputs relative to the α/Table 19-1 convention, and the peak-residency claim '12,095 = synthesis input + O_final' is internally inconsistent with the ledger's own 'Post-call retained context' = 12,095 for the synthesis row whose input is 11,795.
evidence: Ledger row 4 (synthesis): Input before call = 11,795, New model output = 300, Post-call retained context = 12,095. But the text defines 'retained context' as INPUT context (append-only history), and earlier states 'the synthesis call carries 12,095 − 300 = 11,795 as its input prefix' (in the token-quantity table). So post-call retained context after synthesis should be 11,795 (input) — the 300 output is not 'retained context' in the append-only INPUT sense the α framework uses. Yet the ledger lists 12,095 as post-call retained context AND peak residency = 12,095 = 'synthesis input + O_final'. This conflates two definitions: α/Table 19-1 'Total tokens (incl. 300 output)' = 12,095 (which is retained INPUT 11,795 + final output 300), vs the ledger's 'retained context' column which should be pure input. The peak KV residency should be based on the largest INPUT prefix actually held = 11,795 (the synthesis call reads 11,795 tokens), giving 11,795 × 2.62 MB = 30.9 GB, NOT 12,095 × 2.62 MB = 31.7 GB. The book asserts 31.7 GB = Ch 17's I(3), but if I(3) is the input-context residency it should be 11,795. The inclusion of the 300 output tokens in KV residency is questionable: the final 300 output tokens are being generated, and only the already-generated prefix is in KV; at the moment of the synthesis call the KV holds the 11,795 input; the 300 output tokens accumulate during decode. Peak KV = 11,795 (prompt) + up to 300 (generated so far) ≈ 12,095 at the very end of decode — this is defensible IF peak is measured at end-of-decode. But Table 22-1 lists 'KV cache memory per request ~24.9 GB (9.5K max)' using 9,500 (incl output) × 2.62, consistent with counting output in KV. So the book is self-consistent on including output. NOT a discrepancy on the residency number itself. DOWN-GRADED: the ledger is internally consistent with the book's 'incl output' KV convention. However, the label 'Post-call retained context = 12,095' for the synthesis row conflicts with the token-quantity table's 'retained_history = 11,795' for the same synthesis call — same term 'retained' meaning two values (11,795 input vs 12,095 incl output) within adjacent sections. This is a terminology/denominator integrity issue (mechanism 3).
root_cause: The term 'retained context' is used with two denominators: (a) pure input prefix (11,795) in the token-quantity definition table, and (b) input+final-output (12,095) in the event ledger's 'Post-call retained context' column and peak-residency line. Both tie to the α/Table 19-1 'Total tokens (incl. 300 output)' = 12,095, but the ledger column is labeled identically to the input-only 'retained_history' term, inviting a denominator error downstream.
correction: Rename the ledger column 'Post-call retained context (incl. final output)' or split it, and add a one-line note that peak KV residency 12,095 = 11,795 input prefix + 300 generated output at end-of-decode, distinct from the 11,795 input-only retained_history. Ensure 'retained context' always carries its denominator.
acceptance_test: Confirm the synthesis row's two numbers (11,795 input prefix; 12,095 incl. output) are both present and each labeled with its denominator; confirm peak KV 31.7 GB is explicitly tied to the incl-output 12,095 and that Ch 17 I(3) uses the same convention.

quoted_clause: Fallback: 3 attempted turns + single-shot (2%) | ... | Model input tok 39,395 | Model output tok 495 | Total tok 39,890

Completed T=3 task_input = 9,200+10,065+10,930+11,795 = 41,990 (4 calls). The fallback 'attempts the full cap (T=3 — 3 model calls + 3 tool calls) before the guardrail trips, then re-dispatches a single-shot fallback (9,200+300)'. If the fallback makes 3 model calls (turns) but NO terminal synthesis call, its inputs would be calls 1-3 only: 9,200+10,065+10,930 = 30,195, then + single-shot 9,200 = 39,395. ✓ That matches! And output: 3×65 reasoning (195) + single-shot 300 = 495 ✓. Total = 39,395+495 = 39,890 ✓. So the fallback row IS internally consistent: 3 attempted turns (no synthesis) + a fresh single-shot. Recomputed: inputs 9,200+10,065+10,930 = 30,195 (three growing-prefix calls) + 9,200 (single-shot) = 39,395; outputs 65+65+65+300 = 495. CORRECT. NOT a finding on the arithmetic. BUT: the 'Added orchestration 660 ms + ~200 ms ≈ 860 ms' — the 660 ms is 3 turns × 220 ms, but if the fallback never makes a synthesis/4th decision, does it incur 3 full orchestration turns? The completed T=3 also has 660 ms for 3 turns. The fallback does 3 tool round-trips (660 ms) + guardrail/re-dispatch (200 ms) = 860 ms. Consistent. The p99=860ms band claim holds. So this row is arithmetically sound. However, one subtle issue: the completed T=3 row shows task_input 41,990 which INCLUDES the synthesis call input 11,795; the fallback shows 39,395 which EXCLUDES a synthesis call but ADDS a 9,200 single-shot. The difference 41,990 − 39,395 = 2,595 = 11,795 (synthesis input) − 9,200 (single-shot input) = 2,595 ✓. Fully consistent. WITHDRAWN as arithmetic — but note the 'Total tok 39,890' for fallback is LESS than completed T=3 'Total tok 42,485', yet the fallback is presented as the high-cost tail. evidence: Recomputed fallback: 3 growing calls (9,200+10,065+10,930=30,195) + single-shot (9,200) = 39,395 input; outputs 3×65+300 = 495; total 39,890. Matches printed. The completed-T=3 vs fallback difference (42,485 vs 39,890 = 2,595) equals synthesis-input(11,795) − single-shot-input(9,200). All consistent.
root_cause: None — the row is arithmetically correct under the stated '3 attempted turns + single-shot' model. Flagged only to record the rederivation; the apparent 'fallback cheaper than completed T=3' is expected because the fallback skips the expensive synthesis prefill and re-runs a cheaper single-shot.
correction: None required. Optionally add a parenthetical showing the fallback decomposition (30,195 + 9,200) to preempt reader confusion that the tail row is lower than the T=3 row.
acceptance_test: N/A (no defect). If adding the clarifying parenthetical, confirm 39,395 = 30,195 + 9,200 and 495 = 195 + 300.

quoted_clause: with the standalone ρ = 0.95 derate applied to the prefill screen exactly as the policy arithmetic applies it, case (ii) rises to ⌈21.81 / 0.95⌉ = 23 hosts
observed: The text applies the ρ=0.95 derate to the prefill-screen host count 21.81 by DIVIDING (21.81/0.95 = 22.96 → 23), but earlier it applies the SAME ρ=0.95 derate to the KV screen by dividing the per-host RATE denominator (344/(0.95×17) = 21.3 → 22). These are two different applications of ρ to two different screens, which the text acknowledges ('a different 22'). However, the case (ii) prefill screen value 21.81 is itself unverified in this chunk: case (ii) full-square prefill FLOP = 1.5099 PFLOP (Ch 22), and the host-count derivation ⌈21.81⌉ is cited from Ch 17/20 but not recomputed here. The peak prefill demand at 40 rps = 51.5 PFLOP/s (Ch 24 §3.3), and one 8×H100 host = 7.9 PFLOP/s dense peak; at 35% MFU that's 2.765 PFLOP/s/host; 51.5/2.765 = 18.6 hosts (case i, matches '19 hosts under case (i) ⌈18.60⌉'). Under case (ii) full-square, prefill FLOP rises ×1.1723, so hosts = 18.6 × 1.1723 = 21.81 ✓. Then ρ derate: dividing host count by 0.95 (21.81/0.95=22.96→23) treats ρ as reducing effective throughput (more hosts needed) — consistent with the KV-screen treatment (344/(0.95×17)). So the arithmetic is internally consistent. The concern is whether applying ρ to BOTH the KV screen AND the prefill screen double-counts the derate when the final answer takes the max. The text presents 19/21/22/23/32/34 as a menu and says 'the larger requirement wins'. The maximum before full policy is 23; with 70%×95%+N−1 it's 34. This is a planning-screen enumeration, not a single committed number, so double-counting across screens is not a defect per se. MEDIUM confidence because the ρ application to the prefill screen (dividing a host COUNT rather than a rate) is a modeling choice that should be explicitly justified — dividing hosts by ρ assumes the derate scales host count linearly, which holds only if the prefill screen is throughput-limited. It's defensible but under-explained.
evidence: Case (i) prefill: 51.5 PFLOP/s ÷ (7.9×0.35=2.765) = 18.63 → 19 ✓. Case (ii): 18.63×1.1723 = 21.84 ≈ 21.81 ✓ (rounding). ρ derate 21.81/0.95 = 22.96 → 23. KV screen: 344/(0.95×17)=21.3→22. All internally consistent. The only issue is expositional: ρ is applied to the prefill host count by division without stating the assumption that the prefill screen is throughput-bound and ρ reduces effective per-host prefill throughput by 5%.
root_cause: The ρ=0.95 throughput-efficiency derate is applied to the prefill compute screen by dividing the derived host count, mirroring its application to the KV rate screen, but the chunk does not restate WHY dividing host-count-by-ρ is valid for a compute-bound screen (it requires that ρ scale effective prefill throughput). Without that, a reader could misapply ρ to a compute floor that is actually MFU-limited (already at 35%, not efficiency-limited).
correction: Add one sentence: 'ρ=0.95 derates effective per-host throughput, so it divides the host requirement for any throughput-bound screen (KV or prefill); it is not applied to the pure compute floor at the binding MFU.' Or move the ρ-derated prefill number into the policy row only.
acceptance_test: Confirm the chunk states whether ρ applies to the prefill screen as a throughput derate; confirm 23 = ⌈21.81/0.95⌉ and that the final 'larger wins' selection is unambiguous.

quoted_clause: 70B FP16 model footprint — W = N × bytes-per-param = 70 × 10⁹ × 2 B = 140 GB parameters, plus ~30 GB activations at the peak for this worked example, giving ≈ 170 GB total derived footprint. This ~30 GB is a per-request working-set figure ... it is not a re-labeling of the ~64 GB runtime/workspace/NCCL reserve ... (140 GB weights + ~436 GB KV budget + ~64 GB reserve = the 640 GB HBM envelope)
observed: The envelope arithmetic 140 + 436 + 64 = 640 ✓ (matches 8×H100 = 640 GB total HBM). But there is a potential double-count / boundary tension: the ~30 GB per-request activation working set (in the ADR's single-request footprint of 170 GB) is stated to be 'drawn from within that 64 GB workspace line (workspace includes activation buffers)'. Meanwhile the ~436 GB KV budget is the KV cache. The question: at serving time with ~17 concurrent requests, do the per-request activations (30 GB each?) fit in the 64 GB workspace? 30 GB is labeled a single-request peak working set, but 17 concurrent requests would need far more than 64 GB if each truly needed 30 GB of activation buffer simultaneously. The text resolves this by calling 30 GB a 'per-request working-set figure for this ADR's single-request arithmetic' — i.e., not simultaneously resident across all requests. But then the 64 GB workspace reserve cannot hold 17×30 GB. This suggests the 30 GB is a transient peak (e.g., during one request's prefill) not a per-request steady allocation. The text is careful to say the two answer different questions and the envelope closes at 640. However, the coexistence of '~30 GB per-request activations' and '~64 GB total workspace for the whole serving stack' is only consistent if activations are reused/freed between requests (continuous batching), which the text implies ('activation working set is drawn from within that 64 GB workspace'). This is defensible but the 30 GB figure, if read as per-request-resident, would contradict the 64 GB workspace under concurrency. MEDIUM/low severity: the text pre-empts the confusion adequately, but a reader could derive that 17 requests × 30 GB = 510 GB activations > 64 GB workspace, an apparent contradiction. The book should clarify that 30 GB is a transient single-request prefill peak, not a per-request steady-state reservation.
evidence: Envelope 140+436+64 = 640 ✓. But 30 GB/request activation × 17 concurrent = 510 GB would exceed the 64 GB workspace if 30 GB were per-request-resident. The text's single-request framing avoids the contradiction only if activations are transient/reused. The KV budget (436 GB) is separate from activations, so KV is fine; the tension is activations vs workspace.
root_cause: The ~30 GB activation figure is presented as a 'per-request working set' in the ADR footprint (170 GB total) but the 64 GB workspace must serve all concurrent requests. Without stating that the 30 GB is a transient single-request prefill peak (freed/reused across the batch), a reader can construct a contradiction (17×30 GB >> 64 GB).
correction: Clarify that the ~30 GB is the transient peak activation buffer for ONE request's prefill (the ADR's single-request view), reused across the batch within the 64 GB workspace, not a per-request reservation held for all ~17 concurrent requests. Or relabel as 'peak transient activation buffer (single request, reused)'.
acceptance_test: Confirm the chunk states the 30 GB is transient/single-request-reused and that 17×30 GB is not implied to be simultaneously resident within the 64 GB workspace.

quoted_clause: loading the full model weights into HBM takes 30–120 seconds [ILLUSTRATIVE] (a load-path assumption for a ~140 GB model over a ~10–40 Gb/s path — 140 GB ÷ 30–120 s ≈ 4.7–1.2 GB/s — not a hardware benchmark)
observed: The parenthetical has a units inconsistency: it says '~10–40 Gb/s path' (gigabits per second) but then computes '140 GB ÷ 30–120 s ≈ 4.7–1.2 GB/s' (gigabytes per second). 140 GB ÷ 30 s = 4.67 GB/s = 37.3 Gb/s; 140 GB ÷ 120 s = 1.17 GB/s = 9.3 Gb/s. So the implied path is ~9–37 Gb/s, which is roughly consistent with the stated '~10–40 Gb/s' — BUT the intermediate result is written in GB/s (4.7–1.2 GB/s) while the path was stated in Gb/s (10–40 Gb/s), creating an apparent 8× mismatch if a reader doesn't convert. The numbers are actually consistent after bit/byte conversion (4.7 GB/s ≈ 37.6 Gb/s ∈ [10,40]; 1.2 GB/s ≈ 9.6 Gb/s ∈ [10,40]), but mixing Gb/s in the premise and GB/s in the result without noting the conversion is a legibility/units-clarity defect. Given the book's elsewhere-strict units discipline (e.g., the Ch 22 '5.6 TB/s is a rate' note), this mixed-unit parenthetical is a minor inconsistency. Also, 140 GB over PCIe/NVLink: a single H100 has 8×H100 NVLink at 900 GB/s, so 30–120 s for 140 GB implies a much slower path (disk→HBM or single PCIe Gen5 ~14 GB/s), which is plausible for cold start from storage. The '~10–40 Gb/s' (1.25–5 GB/s) is more like a network weight-fetch. The range is plausible for various cold-start paths. LOW severity — units clarity only.
evidence: 140 GB ÷ 30 s = 4.67 GB/s (≈37 Gb/s); 140 GB ÷ 120 s = 1.17 GB/s (≈9.3 Gb/s). Stated path 10–40 Gb/s = 1.25–5 GB/s. The computed 1.17–4.67 GB/s ≈ 9.3–37 Gb/s is close to but slightly outside the stated 10–40 Gb/s at the fast end (37<40 ✓, but 4.67 GB/s stated vs 5 GB/s max). The mix of Gb/s (premise) and GB/s (result) without conversion note is the defect.
root_cause: The parenthetical states the path bandwidth in Gb/s (10–40 Gb/s) but reports the computed transfer rate in GB/s (4.7–1.2 GB/s) without a bit→byte conversion note, inviting an apparent 8× discrepancy. The underlying numbers are consistent after conversion, but the mixed units violate the book's usual units-clarity standard.
correction: State both in the same unit, e.g. 'a ~140 GB model over a ~10–40 Gb/s (1.25–5 GB/s) path — 140 GB ÷ 30–120 s ≈ 1.2–4.7 GB/s (≈10–38 Gb/s)'. Or note '(÷8 for Gb/s)'.
acceptance_test: Confirm the parenthetical uses a single consistent unit (or explicitly converts Gb/s↔GB/s) and that 140 GB ÷ {30,120}s matches the stated path bandwidth.

quoted_clause: Under a 100% prefix-reuse policy only the incremental prefix (9,200 + 3×865 = 11,795) is pre-filled, giving W_reuse(3) ≈ 14.16 s
observed: Under 100% prefix reuse, only the incremental prefix 9,200 + 3×865 = 11,795 is pre-filled ONCE (the base 9,200 + each turn's 865 new tokens). Prefill = (11,795/9,200)×1.08 = 1.282×1.08 = 1.385 s. Decode = 0.025×495 = 12.375 s. Tool = 3×0.133 = 0.399 s. Sum = 1.385+12.375+0.399 = 14.159 ≈ 14.16 s ✓. Correct. But wait — under 100% prefix reuse, is the decode still 495 tokens? Yes, all generated tokens must still be decoded. And the prefill is only the unique tokens 11,795 (each token pre-filled once). ✓. The no-reuse prefill was 4.93 s (41,990 re-prefilled); reuse prefill 1.385 s; difference = 3.54 s = the re-prefill savings. Consistent. NOT a finding. The Table 22-1 and Ch 19 reuse W(3)=14.16 matches. Recorded for coverage.

quoted_clause: decode required BW rate | ~5.6 TB/s | ~140 GB / 25 ms TPOT ... under the canonical 8×H100 tensor-parallel host the 140 GB is sharded, so each GPU streams only ~0.70 TB/s against its own 3.35 TB/s

The text correctly notes the shard-invariant reason decode is memory-limited is low arithmetic intensity (~1 FLOP/byte), not the raw 5.6>3.35 comparison (which would be wrong since 5.6 TB/s aggregate vs 8×3.35=26.8 TB/s aggregate headroom). The '~140 GB weight-read per token' = full 70B×2B = 140 GB read every token (no activation reuse) — the classic decode bandwidth bound. ✓. evidence: 140 GB/0.025 s = 5.6 TB/s; /8 = 0.70 TB/s/GPU; 0.70/3.35 = 21%. Correct. Low-arithmetic-intensity framing correct.

quoted_clause: the single-region arithmetic gives ~$155.8K/mo (~$24.97/1K) self-host, ~$87.6K/mo (~$14.04/1K) ... and ~$129.8K/mo (~$20.8/1K) managed API at the canonical 6.24M requests/mo
observed: Self-host: $24.97/1K × 6.24M/1000 = 24.97066... × 6,240 = $155,817 ≈ $155.8K ✓ (matches Ch 16/22's $24.97/1K). Cloud: $14.04/1K × 6,240 = $87,609 ≈ $87.6K ✓ (14.038461538 × 6,240 = 87,600). Managed: $20.8/1K × 6,240 = $129,792 ≈ $129.8K ✓. 6.24M req/mo = 10 rps × 8h × 3600 × 260 / ... let me verify: 10 × 3600 × 8 × 260 = 75,840,000/mo? No: 10 rps × 3600 s/h × 8 h/day × 260 day = 75,840,000. That's 75.84M, not 6.24M. Wait — Ch 19/21 says '~6.24M/month — Ch 4's 8-h × 260-workday calendar basis'. Let me recompute: 10 rps × 3600 s/h = 36,000 req/h; × 8 h = 288,000 req/workday; × 260 workdays = 74,880,000/mo = 74.88M. That's NOT 6.24M. Hmm. But Ch 21 §3 says '288,000 requests/workday ... ~6.24M/month'. 288,000 × 260 = 74,880,000. So 6.24M is WRONG if 288,000/workday × 260. UNLESS 6.24M = 288,000 × 21.67 days, or 6.24M = 288,000 × ... 6,240,000 / 288,000 = 21.67 workdays. That's not 260/12=21.67! 260 workdays/year ÷ 12 months = 21.67 workdays/month. So 6.24M/month = 288,000/workday × 21.67 workdays/month = 6,240,000 ✓. The 260 is ANNUAL workdays; monthly = 260/12 = 21.67. So 6.24M/mo is correct on a monthly basis (260 annual workdays / 12). And Ch 21's '~6.24M/month — Ch 4's 8-h × 260-workday calendar basis' — the annual is 288,000 × 260 = 74.88M/year ÷ 12 = 6.24M/month ✓. Consistent! So 6.24M/mo is correct. The $/1K × 6,240 (=6.24M/1000) all check out. NOT a finding. Good — this was a potential false positive I caught and resolved (mechanism #5 false-positive defense: benign-interpretation challenge — the 260 is annual, monthly is /12). Recorded for coverage.
evidence: 288,000 req/workday × 260 workdays/yr = 74.88M/yr ÷ 12 = 6.24M/mo ✓. $24.97×6,240=$155.8K; $14.04×6,240=$87.6K; $20.8×6,240=$129.8K. All verified. The 6.24M monthly basis = annual 260 workdays /12.
root_cause: None — verified. The 6.24M/mo is the monthly average of the 260-annual-workday calendar (74.88M/yr ÷ 12). Initially looked like a 288,000×260=74.88M discrepancy but resolves to monthly basis.
correction: None. Optionally add '/12 (monthly average of 260 annual workdays)' next to 6.24M to preempt the same confusion.
